stem: What is the molecular shape of XeF₄?

rationales.A: Square pyramidal needs five bonds and one lone pair (as in IF₅). XeF₄ has four bonds and two lone pairs, so the lone pairs sit opposite each other and the shape is square planar.
rationales.B: Tetrahedral requires four bonds and no lone pairs. XeF₄ has two lone pairs on opposite sides of xenon, so the four F atoms lie in a flat square, not a tetrahedron.
rationales.C: Correct. Xenon has 8 valence electrons; four Xe–F bonds use 4, leaving 4 (two lone pairs). The six electron pairs place the two lone pairs opposite each other, leaving the four F atoms in a square plane.
rationales.D: Seesaw is the shape with four bonds and one lone pair, as in SF₄. XeF₄ has two lone pairs on xenon, which sit opposite each other and give a square planar shape.

stem: What is the molecular shape of BrF₃?

rationales.A: Trigonal planar would need three bonds and no lone pairs. BrF₃ also has two lone pairs on bromine, which push the F atoms into a T with angles near 90°, not 120°.
rationales.B: Seesaw requires four bonds and one lone pair (as in SF₄). BrF₃ has three bonds and two lone pairs, so the shape is T-shaped.
rationales.C: This counts only one lone pair on bromine, as in NF₃. Bromine has two lone pairs, so the molecule is T-shaped.
rationales.D: Correct. Bromine has 7 valence electrons; three Br–F bonds use 3, leaving 4 (two lone pairs). The five electron pairs place both lone pairs in equatorial positions, leaving three F atoms in a T-shape.
